confirmed.description: Varma's seat changes from a floor mat to a throne chair partway through the audience, and the lettering still calls it a mat. In 2.1 and 2.2 he sits cross-legged on a mat and cushion on the low wooden platform, as the script asks. From 3.4 on he sits in a raised carved chair with his feet on a footstool. On page 6 that chair is also two different thrones: a gilded red chair in 6.1, then a dark wood throne with carved lion armrests in 6.4. The lion throne returns in 8.5 and 10.2.
confirmed.evidence: 3.4: tall carved wooden chair with a red seat and a footstool. 6.1: red upholstered chair at the top of three steps. 6.4 and 8.5: lion-head armrests. The 10.2 balloon says "He has spent too many lives to sit on that mat" next to a visible lion armrest. 8.5 is scripted as the spear butt tapping "against the mat", but it hits the floor below a throne.

verdict.reason: I confirmed this in the art. In 2.1 and 2.2, Varma sits cross-legged on a mat on the low wooden platform, with the map spread on the mat in front of him, as the script asks. In 3.4 he sits in a tall carved chair with a red seat, his feet on a footstool. In 6.1 (cropped) it is a gilded, red-upholstered chair at the top of steps, with his legs hanging down. In 6.4 (cropped) it is a dark carved throne with lion-head armrests. 8.5 (cropped) shows the same lion throne, and the spear butt taps the floor in front of it. In 10.2 (cropped) a gold lion-head armrest shows between Varma and Ramayyan, right next to the balloon "He has spent too many lives to sit on that mat." The script never allows a chair or throne. It calls for "a slightly raised wooden platform," a map "on the mat before him," and in 8.5 a spear tapped "against the mat." So the seat changes partway through one audience, takes two different forms on page 6 alone, and contradicts the 10.2 line about "that mat." It also works against the page 2 caption that contrasts the grand Deccan halls with this hall. This is a clear continuity and prop error that the lettering points straight at, but it involves no identity, forbidden content or missing beat, so it is major, not a blocker. The fix is to redraw Varma seated on the platform mat in 3.3, 3.4, 6.1, 6.2, 6.4, 8.5 and 10.2, and check 9.5 for the same throne. I did not look at 9.5 myself.

confirmed.description: Balloons hide most of the hearsay stain and the king's beat. The script wants only two things in the stain: the padre and a column of Portuguese musketeers. Only one musketeer shows, half hidden behind the padre's shoulder and the upper balloon. The rest of the column, and with it the broad hats and buff coats that tell them apart from Dutch or British troops, sits under the lettering. Varma's hand tapping the spear shaft at the foreground edge is also lost: the right edge shows only a strip of his gold-bordered cloth and a few necklace beads behind the lower balloon.
confirmed.evidence: Crop of 4.4: one buff-coated figure with a matchlock beside the padre, nothing else of the column. The right edge shows cream-and-gold cloth and beads, with no hand and no spear shaft.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on page 4, panel 4.4. In the r3 render, both NAGOJI balloons fill the right half of the panel. All that shows of the column is one buff-coated figure with a matchlock half behind the padre's shoulder and a sliver of hat brim. At the right edge there is only a dark pole tip, a brown diagonal with gold beads, and cream-and-gold cloth. No hand can be read tapping the shaft. The script (4.4) asks for both things: a column of musketeers in broad tilted hats and buff coats, and Varma's hand tapping the spear shaft at the foreground edge. Its notes repeat that the Portuguese at 4.4 wear broad hats and buff coats.

The unlettered frame (chapters/ch06/frames/page-04-panel-04-v02.png) shows that the art itself is correct. It has a full receding column of about ten musketeers in plumed broad hats and buff coats, and Varma's ringed forearm and hand gripping the dark spear shaft at the right edge. The beat was lost in layout, through the crop and scale of the panel and where the balloons sit, not in the drawing.

That makes this a localized balloon-placement and crop problem that hides scripted action, which the rubric rates major. The core image still reads (padre ahead, an armed soldier behind) and the fix needs no redraw, so it is not a blocker. It could be fixed by stacking the balloons over the plain smoke and sky at the upper left and center, or by refitting the crop so the column and the hand on the shaft stay clear.

confirmed.description: Wrong speaker tail: Nagoji's narration balloon 'Our clerks said their padres walk ahead of the soldiers...' has its tail aimed straight at the padre in the stain image, so the padre seems to be speaking.
confirmed.evidence: In the top-right balloon of 4.4, the tail tip lands on the padre's waist and hand below his raised cross. Nagoji is seated at lower left. Only the second balloon ('We heard of rajas...') points toward him.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. The problem is real on page 4, panel 4.4 (file page-04.png). The script makes both lines in this panel NAGOJI dialogue. Nagoji sits at lower left, and the padre in the stain is only a hearsay image, not a speaker. On the crop, the top-right balloon ('Our clerks said their padres walk ahead...') has a long tail that points down and to the left. Its tip ends right on the padre's belt and waist, just under his raised cross arm. It points nowhere near Nagoji. Only the second balloon ('We heard of rajas...') points at Nagoji, from roughly his shoulder height. The tail is big and clear, so it will still be obvious at print size. Readers take the first balloon first, so the padre seems to be speaking. The words 'their padres' make that odd, which only forces a double-take. Nothing in the script or bible allows a tail on a figure inside a stain. The fix is localized: re-aim the first tail at Nagoji, for example down the left side of the balloon past the padre toward his head, or join it to the second balloon. That makes this major (wrong speaker tail), not blocker.

confirmed.description: The two large balloons cover the key action of this panel. The script calls for a column of Portuguese musketeers behind the padre and Varma's hand tapping the spear shaft at the foreground edge. The balloons hide the column and the tap.
confirmed.evidence: Only one musketeer shows, half behind the right edge of the upper balloon. The lower balloon covers the right foreground edge, where Varma's gold-bordered cloth and a gold ornament peek out, so no hand-on-shaft tap can be read. The two balloons fill about the right 45% of the panel.

verdict.reason: The finding holds. The unlettered frame (chapters/ch06/frames/page-04-panel-04-v02.png) has the full beat. It shows about ten Portuguese musketeers in broad plumed hats and buff coats with matchlocks, marching behind the padre at roughly 50-82% of the frame width. It also shows Varma's hand with a gold bead bracelet gripping a dark spear shaft with a brass ferrule at the right foreground edge. In the lettered render (page-04.png, panel 4.4) the upper balloon ("Our clerks said...") covers the whole musketeer column. Only one soldier's hat brim, shoulder and matchlock show at the balloon's left edge. The lower balloon ("We heard of rajas...") covers the hand and the shaft. Only a sliver of the gold beads, part of the shaft and the gold-bordered cloth show at the right edge, so the tap cannot be read at all. The script calls this the page's biggest panel and says it holds "only two things", the padre and the column, plus the hand-on-shaft tap. Lettering hides the column and the whole tap, so it is not slight. The severity is major, not blocker: the art is correct and nothing needs redrawing. The fix is local to lettering. Move or shrink the balloons into the empty smoke and pillar area at upper left, over the haze above Nagoji, or stack them at upper left and centre-top so the column and the right-edge hand stay clear.

confirmed.description: Ramayyan's second balloon ('How their forts stand...') covers his pointing hand and stylus. The panel's action is Ramayyan pointing with the stylus to the mat, and that action is hidden.
confirmed.evidence: Ramayyan's outstretched right arm runs down-right from his shoulder and vanishes behind the big balloon around mid-panel. No hand or stylus can be seen pointing at the mat at lower right. The balloon also hides most of his body.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. In the page 4, panel 4.2 crop, Ramayyan's outstretched forearm runs down-right from his sleeve. It goes behind the tail of the second balloon and then behind the balloon itself ('How their forts stand...'), at about mid-height on the left of the panel. His hand never comes back into view, and no stylus can be seen anywhere in the panel. Only his other hand shows, holding a closed palm-leaf bundle at his hip. The balloon also covers most of his torso and lower body. Script 4.2 asks for him 'pointing with his stylus to a mat', and the page note puts weight on the diwan's stylus, so the scripted prop and the end of the gesture are lost. I am rating it minor rather than major for three reasons. First, the beat still reads: his arm clearly reaches toward Nagoji and the mat, the mat is fully visible at lower centre, and Nagoji is clearly lowering himself onto it with bandaged hands. Second, the 'Sit.' balloon makes the instruction plain. Third, the stylus motif is shown fully in the 4.5 inset (and later in 5.3 and 6.2), so the page's stylus payoff is not lost. This is a localized balloon-placement problem to polish: moving or shrinking the second balloon, for example into the open floor or wall area, would reveal the hand and stylus. It does not hide a story beat.

confirmed.description: Wrong speaker tail: Ramayyan's line 'Take the Madurai horse and a hundred Maravar riders...' points at Varma, so the king seems to say it in Konkani. That breaks the rule that Varma's only lettered word is 'Ram.'
confirmed.evidence: The tail of the large lower-centre balloon rises to the hem of Varma's cream-and-gold cloth at his right knee. Ramayyan sits further right; the second balloon ('If you are wrong...') points to him correctly.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. In panel 9.5 the large lower-centre balloon ("Take the Madurai horse and a hundred Maravar riders...") points to Varma. Its tail runs up and to the right and its tip ends on the gold-fringed end of Varma's draped cream-and-gold cloth at his left knee, at about px (1230,2285) in the 1838x2775 render. The tip lands clearly inside Varma's figure. Ramayyan's white dhoti begins about 40-50 px further right, so the tail never reaches him. It still reads this way when the page is scaled down to print size. Reading left to right, the left balloon goes to the left seated figure (the king) and the right balloon ("If you are wrong...") goes to Ramayyan, whose tail is correct. This attribution is wrong. Script 9.5 gives both lines to RAMAYYAN. The chapter's lettering convention (script line 73 and the note at line 364) says Varma speaks only through "[in Malayalam]" tag balloons, and his only lettered word in the chapter is "Ram." Neither the bible nor the script allows this. The fix is local: re-aim the first balloon's tail past Varma to Ramayyan, for example to his lap or shoulder, or merge it with the second balloon. That makes it a major wrong-speaker-tail issue, not a blocker.

confirmed.description: The two balloons sit over the moment the panel exists for: horses coming in at an angle and the Portuguese line breaking.
confirmed.evidence: The upper balloon covers Kanka's legs and the water where the charging horses meet the line. The lower balloon covers the lower half of the stumbling and falling musketeers in the centre-right. What stays visible is the riders' upper bodies at top and the standing musketeers at far right.

verdict.reason: This is partly right but overstated, so I am downgrading it from major to minor. In the full-resolution crop of panel 8.2 (page-08.png, panel at about x242-1598, y718-1523), the upper balloon does sit on Kanka from the mid-chest down. It hides her forelegs, the rider's lower leg and the water where she would land. That is a real cost, since the dialogue talks about "a hoof" and the hero mare's hooves are not shown. The beat still reads clearly, though. The angled charge is visible at left and top: several turbaned riders, horse legs and splashing water, and Nagoji on Kanka with her head, mane and bridle shown. The breaking Portuguese line is also plainly visible at right. One musketeer reels back with his matchlock, one doubles over, one has fallen into the barrels in the bottom-right corner, and more figures scatter in the background. One rider (white turban, centre-right) is shown actually reaching the musketeers, so the moment of contact is not hidden. The claim about the lower balloon is mostly inaccurate. It covers foreground water and sand between present-day Nagoji and the line, and only clips the knees of the bending musketeer; the fallen musketeer at bottom right is fully visible. The script also asks for the speech to be broken across the memory image, and two long balloons in this busy panel have to cover something. The best fix is to nudge the upper balloon left or down so Kanka's forelegs show; this is polish, not a localized error that needs a redraw.

confirmed.description: Awkward crop: in a very short full-width strip the top border slices off Varma's turban, so the jewelled peacock-feather crest (a visual lock in every Varma panel) is lost. The 'Ram.' balloon sits beside a head with no crown.
confirmed.evidence: Only the lower band of the turban shows at the top edge above Varma's brow. The crest and feather, visible in every other Varma panel in the chapter, are out of frame. The panel is only about 346 px tall at 1838 px width.

verdict.reason: The problem is real on page 8, panel 8.5, but I rate it minor rather than major. At full resolution the panel runs from about y=2195 to y=2540, so it is about 345 px tall across the page width. The top border cuts straight across Varma's forehead at brow and tilak level. Only the lower front band of the cream-and-gold turban shows, at the left temple and above the right ear. The top of the turban and the jeweled peacock-feather crest are entirely out of frame. The script for 8.5 asks for the crest, and the bible's formal court audience look includes it, so neither one allows this crop. Why it is not major: the face, mustache, pearl earrings, necklaces, spear, the two tap ticks, the bird on the parapet and the "Ram." balloon with its tail on Varma are all clearly readable. Identity and the beat land. The costume is cropped rather than wrong, and the action is not hidden. It is still a visible head-against-the-border tangent on the page's closing panel. The fix is a re-crop or a slightly taller strip with Varma placed lower, so the crest fits.

confirmed.description: The two captions cover the horizon they refer to. 'Somewhere beyond that horizon sat Goa' sits over the very line it names. The art left almost no sky band, against the script's instruction to keep the sky open for two captions.
confirmed.evidence: The left caption runs across about x 118-710 and the right one across about x 835-1420 of a 1540 px panel crop. Both sit flush against the top border and reach down to the waterline. The horizon shows only in a gap of about 125 px between them.

verdict.reason: The facts check out, but I rate this minor, not major. I cropped panel 7.5 on page 7 (about 1540x320 px). The sky band is only about 90 px tall, and the horizon sits about 110 px below the top border. The left caption ("Somewhere beyond that horizon sat Goa...") runs from about y 20 to 148. The right caption ("Somewhere farther still, Dutch hulls...") runs from about y 20 to 188. Both start at the top border and reach past the horizon into the upper sea. The horizon is visible only in a gap of about 125 px between them (x ~718-843). Pillars and palms hide it at both edges. The right caption also clips the mast tops of the right-hand boat. So the art ignores the script's instruction to "keep the sky open for two captions", and the captions cover most of the horizon they point to. Why not major: both captions are fully legible and nothing in the beat is lost. The shore, the men with sacks and nets, all three boats and the flat sea all read clearly. A piece of hard horizon still shows between the boxes, so "beyond that horizon" still has something to point to, about 0.4 in wide at a print width of roughly 5 in. This is a caption-placement and composition problem that weakens the empty-horizon mood. Fixes: narrower or shorter caption boxes, or a re-render with a taller sky. No identity, costume or action is hidden.

confirmed.description: Wrong speaker tail: Nagoji's hearsay line "Our clerks said their padres walk ahead of the soldiers..." has its tail ending on the padre's body in the stain image, so the padre seems to be speaking.
confirmed.evidence: page-04.png, upper balloon (about x 680-1050, y 1020-1220 in the 1325-wide view). Its tail tip lands on the black cassock at the padre's waist (about x 610, y 1160). Nagoji, the real speaker, is seated at lower left (about x 340-580, y 1210-1470).

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 4, panel 4.4. In the zoomed crop, the upper balloon ("Our clerks said their padres walk ahead...") has a long, distinct tail whose tip sits right on the padre's belt or sash, at about x 610, y 1160 in the 1325-wide view. The padre is the largest, most clearly drawn figure in the stain, with his face and body fully visible, so the tail makes him read as the speaker. The script gives both lines in 4.4 to Nagoji, who sits lower left. The lower balloon's tail correctly points to Nagoji, but the upper balloon has its own separate tail rather than a connector chained to the lower balloon, so it does not borrow that attribution. The third-person wording ("their padres") helps a careful reader work out the speaker, but at print size the misattribution is plain at first glance. This is a wrong speaker tail, so it is major, not a blocker: the lettering can be fixed by pointing the tail at Nagoji or linking it to the lower balloon, with no redraw needed.

confirmed.description: The hearsay stain loses half of its beat, and the framing is reversed. Script 4.4 calls for an anonymous padre leading a column of Portuguese musketeers (broad tilted hats, buff coats, matchlocks), with Nagoji small at the lower edge. It should be the page's biggest panel, with Varma's hand tapping the spear shaft at the foreground edge. The render shows only the padre and one partly hidden figure behind him, mostly covered by the balloon, so there is no column of musketeers for 'the men behind count how many guns' to refer to. Nagoji is large and fills the left foreground. The panel is narrower than 4.5 and no larger than it. No Varma hand or tap appears.
confirmed.evidence: page-04.png, panel 4.4 (x 268-1058, y 1015-1488). Behind the padre there is a single shadowy soldier at about x 660-720, y 1100-1250, cut off by the balloon. The right edge has only a sliver of gold-bordered cloth and a dark shaft, with no hand on it. Nagoji takes up about a third of the panel at x 340-580.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on page-04.png, panel 4.4 (about x 372-1470, y 1415-2067 at full resolution). Script 4.4 asks for a stain showing an anonymous padre leading a column of musketeers in broad hats, buff coats and matchlocks. Nagoji should be small at the lower edge, Varma's hand should tap the spear shaft at the foreground edge, and this should be the page's biggest panel.

What the render shows:
(1) The padre is correct: plain black cassock, no collar tab, cross held high, a stranger's face.
(2) Only one musketeer is readable: buff coat, matchlock, and a hat brim just peeking past the upper balloon. The rest is a few legs and gun butts that the two balloons almost entirely cover. There is no readable column for "the men behind count how many guns" to point to.
(3) Nagoji is a large foreground figure taking up about a third of the panel width on the left. The stain is pushed back behind him, so the intended emphasis is inverted.
(4) At the right edge, a brown diagonal limb or shaft with gold beads (probably Varma's braceleted forearm, which the cast override, nagoji plus varma, supports) and a dark vertical shaft can be seen. The hand and the tap itself are hidden under the lower balloon, so the tap does not read.
(5) The panel's area (about 790x470 display px) is roughly equal to 4.5 (about 1110x340), so it is not the page's dominant panel.

Why major and not blocker: the core idea, a padre walking ahead of armed soldiers, still reads at print size. But the column, Nagoji's small scale and Varma's tap are clearly wrong and confined to this panel. Moving the balloons or re-cropping would fix part of it (the tap and the musketeers may be under the lettering), and a re-render would fix the Nagoji scale.

One correction to the original evidence: the right edge shows more than "a sliver of cloth and a shaft". A braceleted arm is partly visible, but no hand, so the conclusion stands.

confirmed.description: The king's seat changes from the scripted mat to a throne. Script 2.2 puts Varma on a slightly raised wooden platform with the map on the mat before him; 8.5 has him tap his spear against the mat; and 10.2 says he has 'spent too many lives to sit on that mat'. The chapter's premise ('They did not take me to a palace') depends on this. 2.1 and 2.2 draw it that way, but from 2.5 on he sits on a tall carved throne chair with lion armrests and red cushions, on a dais several steps high. The same platform is drawn two different ways, and the 10.2 line no longer matches the art.
confirmed.evidence: page-02.png 2.2: cross-legged on a mat on a low platform. page-02.png 2.5 (about x 1000-1090, y 1640-1700): throne at the top of a stepped dais. page-03.png 3.4: carved throne chair with red cushion and a footstool. page-06.png 6.1 and 6.4: lion-armrest throne on a three-step dais. page-08.png 8.5 and page-09.png 9.5: the same throne.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute this. The art shows the problem, and neither the script nor the bible allows it. The script calls for "a slightly raised wooden platform" with the map "on the mat before him" (2.2). At 8.5 he "taps the butt of his spear against the mat". At 10.2 the lettered line reads "He has spent too many lives to sit on that mat." CONTINUITY.md never mentions a throne, and its Varma entry covers only dress. Pages 2.1 and 2.2 follow the script: he sits cross-legged on a mat on a low wooden platform, with the map in front of him. From 2.5 on, the seat changes.
- 2.5 (zoomed crop): a tall carved seat with a red back and cushions, at the top of a four-step stone dais, with standing guards and lamps on both sides. On the same page it reads as a different place from 2.2.
- 3.3: red round cushioned armrests.
- 3.4: a carved chair with a red cushion. His legs hang down and his feet rest on a footstool.
- 6.1: the chair sits high on a multi-step dais above Nagoji's mat.
- 6.4: carved lion armrests.
- 8.5: lion-head armrests. The spear butt taps the floor beside the throne, not a mat.
- 9.5: the throne again, on steps.
The 10.2 balloon ("sit on that mat") is letter-perfect to the script. It no longer matches anything the reader has seen since page 2. The change also weakens the chapter's premise in the page-1 caption, "They did not take me to a palace", and the page-2 caption that contrasts Deccan high halls with this one. This is a clear prop and setting error, and it is consistent across about nine panels. Identity, content and the beats are all intact, and the lettering is readable. So I rate it major, not blocker. The fix is to redraw the king's seat in the hall panels from 2.5 onward as a low mat on a low wooden platform. The other option is to change the 10.2 line and accept that 2.2 and 2.5 disagree, which is weaker.

refuted.description: Ramayyan's off-panel line 'They questioned you.' has a tail that points up to the top border just right of where Varma's arm enters, so it reads as Varma speaking. Varma's only lettered words in the chapter should be 'Ram.', so this undercuts the chapter's lettering convention.
refuted.reason: I cropped panel 3.5 from the 300 DPI render. The tail of "They questioned you." does not lead to Varma. The arm comes in through the top border about 100 to 330 px from the panel's left edge. The tail tip sits about 557 px in, roughly 230 px (about 0.75 in at print) to the right of the arm. It points straight up into empty background over the lamp, between the king's hand on the left and Nagoji on the right. That is where panel 3.4 just placed Ramayyan, at his low table between Varma and Nagoji, so an upward off-panel tail at that spot fits his position. The figure elements the reviewer mentions are the cream-and-gold cloth at the far left edge and the arm entering top-left. Varma's off-panel head would therefore be above and to the left, not where the tail points. Context also settles the speaker. In 3.3, on the same page, the king's speech is set only as the "[in Malayalam]" tag, so readers already know that plain English lines come through the diwan. "They questioned you." also continues Ramayyan's second-person questions from 3.4 ("You raided Portuguese outposts..."). Using a plain tail to the border for an off-panel speaker is standard lettering, and the script marks this line "RAMAYYAN (off)". The art does not misattribute the line, so I am refuting it.

refuted.description: The page does not sit on a grid. Each of the five rows is a different width and none reaches the page margins, so the page reads as a stack of floating images rather than the gridded page of the approved Chapter 1. The script also asks for 8.2 to run full width.
refuted.reason: I'm rejecting this. The measurements are right, but the reason given is not. Page 8 does have five rows of different widths: 330-1507, 241-1596, 516-1320, 268-1568 and 205-1632. None of them reaches the 148-1688 margins. But the claim that the approved Chapter 1 always sits on that grid is false. Ch1 r6 page 6 stacks three middle rows at 207-1630, 414-1422 and 261-1575, and it reads exactly like this page: a floating stack of centred rows of different widths. Inset rows centred on the page are the compositor's normal way of fitting art at its own aspect ratio, used on almost every chapter. Ch1 pages 2-8 have them. Ch2 r4 page 1 has no row reaching the margins at all (187-1650, 207-1629, 318-1518). Ch3, Ch4 and Ch5 have them, and so do Ch6 pages 3, 4, 5, 7 and 9. So this is house layout, not a broken grid. On the script: 8.3 is supposed to be narrow, so its narrow width is correct. 8.2 is still clearly the page's dominant panel. It is about 37% of the live height, against the script's "about 40 percent", and it is 88% of the full width. 8.5 is the widest row on the page and falls short by only about 57 px (about 0.19 in) each side. What's left is a small polish choice: the art could be cropped so 8.2 and 8.5 run truly full width and anchor the page, as Ch1 page 6 does with its top and bottom rows. That is minor at most, and well short of major.

refuted.description: Wrong speaker tail: Ramayyan's line "Take the Madurai horse and a hundred Maravar riders..." points to Varma, so the king appears to speak in English. The chapter's convention is that Varma's only lettered word is "Ram".
refuted.reason: I'm refuting this. It is not a wrong-speaker tail. At full resolution, the left balloon's tail on page 9, panel 9.5 runs from its base at about (1168, 2337) to its tip at about (1227, 2278) in the 1838x2775 image. That is a clean 45-degree line up and to the right. If you extend that line, it reaches the height of the faces (y about 2020-2050) at x about 1450-1480. That is Ramayyan's head, at about x 1400-1450. Varma's head is at about x 1115, roughly 330 px left of the line, and the tail angles away from him. The reviewer is right that the tip stops short. It lands on the gold-bordered cloth hanging from Varma's throne arm, about 60 px left of Ramayyan's white dhoti. But a tail is read by where it points, and this one points at Ramayyan. Context supports him as the speaker too. The script gives both 9.5 lines to Ramayyan. Every Varma line in the chapter is a small "[in Malayalam]" balloon, and the very next balloon has a clear tail to Ramayyan. Viewed at print size, the tail reads as heading toward the diwan, not toward the king's face. At most this is a lettering polish note: lengthen the tail tip by about 60-80 px along the same angle so it clears Varma's drape and ends near Ramayyan.

refuted.description: Nagoji (and apparently Ibrahim) look seated or crouched among the courtiers during the whisper, with forearms folded across raised knees. In the script they are still entering, and in the very next shot (2.5) Nagoji walks into the clear space. The art shows him already settled before he walks in.
refuted.reason: I cropped and zoomed page 2, panel 2.3 (original px about x 920-1695, y 1300-1595). The bottom strip does show Nagoji's two bandaged forearms held forward and level over cream cloth. But nothing else in the panel shows him seated. His head sits at about the eye line of the standing guards near the platform, and well above the heads of the seated courtiers behind him, so the perspective puts him at standing height. Everything between his shoulders and forearms is hidden by the "Remember what I said about gifts" balloon, so the pose cannot be read either way. Ibrahim is not seated at all: he leans in to Nagoji's ear with his hand on the coat pocket, as the script asks. Script 2.3 only calls for a close shot with Ibrahim at Nagoji's ear and Nagoji in profile, listening. It does not say they are mid-stride. A short pause just inside the hall while Ibrahim briefs him reads naturally between 2.1 (entering) and 2.5 (walking down the lane). Neither CONTINUITY.md nor the cast overrides say anything about posture here. At print size the forearms are a thin band under a balloon, and the panel reads as two men huddled in a whisper, so this is too slight and too ambiguous to count as a continuity error. At most it is optional polish.

minors.description: Nagoji's ear ornament is drawn as a hanging gold drop or bead earring in every panel where it shows. The bible and the author decision of 2026-10-02 require a small, flush gold stud. The author logged this as a known deviation for ch1 to 8, so it goes on the list for the author and is not a redraw trigger.
minors.evidence: Crops of 1.2, 1.4, 5.2, 8.4 and 10.1 show a round gold bead hanging below the lobe on a short post. In 8.4 (profile) the drop is especially clear. In 5.2 and 10.1 there is one on each ear.

minors.description: Nagoji's chin and jaw carry visible stubble stippling. The bible says CLEAN-SHAVEN CHIN, with light stubble allowed only in captivity, and ch6 is not captivity.
minors.evidence: A zoomed crop of the 8.4 profile shows dark stipple across the chin and along the jawline below the moustache. In the other ch6 close-ups (1.4, 4.3, 5.2, 6.3) the chin is smooth.

minors.description: Nagoji's chin is shaded grey-dark with a darker patch under the lower lip, which reads as stubble or a soul patch on a character who must be clean-shaven.
minors.evidence: Zoomed crop of Nagoji's face in 10.1 ("As he commands."): the chin has a grey stubble cast and a dark mark under the lip. Compare 5.2, where the same frontal angle has a clean chin.

minors.description: The speaking gate guard (screen right) is built on Nagoji's face formula: strong cheekbones, a thick curled moustache, a clean chin and a small ear stud, with a topknot. Next to Nagoji in the same panel he reads as a look-alike, and he anticipates Nagoji's later Ananthan Pillai topknot look.
minors.evidence: A crop of the guard under the balloon "The king is in council. You are expected." shows a heavy upturned curled moustache, a shaven chin, a small pale stud in the ear and a topknot. The other guards and grooms in ch6 have beards or plain moustaches.

minors.description: Ramayyan's naming panel crops the top of his head at the panel border, so his main sheet identifier, the receding or balding crown, never shows. Only dark curls at the sides are visible, and he reads younger and fuller-haired than the gaunt, balding Ramayyan of 2.2, 3.3, 4.2 and 9.3.
minors.evidence: In 2.4 the top border cuts across his upper forehead. The sheet 03-ramayyan-dalawa-v15.png and his appearances in 2.2, 3.1, 3.3 and 5.3 all show a bald crown with a curly fringe at the sides.

minors.description: Same crop problem as 2.4. Ramayyan's head is cut at the panel top, and the curls at the edge read as a full head of hair rather than his receding hairline. With the king out of frame, this is the panel where his identity has to carry alone.
minors.evidence: In the crop of 9.1 ("The Madurai horsemen know the straight charge..."), thick black curls sit above the forehead at the border and no bald crown is visible. In 9.2 and 9.3, on the same page, he is clearly balding.

minors.description: Varma's head touches the panel top, which cuts off his turban, so the jewelled peacock-feather crest required for this formal audience is lost. On the "Ram." beat the king barely reads in his court look.
minors.evidence: In the zoomed crop of 8.5, only the lower band of the cream turban and a hint of gold show above his brow before the border. There is no crest and no feather. Compare 2.2, 4.1, 5.5 and 9.5, where the crest is clear.

minors.description: In profile, Varma's turban shows no jewelled crest or peacock feather because its front is cut by the panel top. His cheek and jaw also carry stubble stippling, which the varma-v1 sheet does not show (moustache only).
minors.evidence: The zoomed crop of 9.4 shows a plain cream turban with a gold band, no crest, and stippled stubble across the cheek and jaw down to the moustache.

minors.description: Nagoji's waist changes between panels on the same page. In 10.3 a white cloth sash is knotted around his waist over the shirt. In 10.4 and 10.5 the shirt hangs loose over the dhoti and a plain dhoti knot sits below the hem, as the script asks (NO sash). 2.1 also shows the same white cummerbund-style wrap over the shirt.
minors.evidence: 10.3: a white band wrapped over the cream shirt at the waist. 10.4: the shirt hem falls over the dhoti, with the knot below and no sash.

minors.description: Nagoji's ear ornament is a hanging gold drop, not the small flush stud the bible requires. In 5.2 and 10.1 he wears one in both ears. This is the known ch1 to 8 deviation the author asked to have listed rather than reopened automatically.
minors.evidence: Drops are visible at 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 2.3, 3.3, 3.4, 5.1, 5.2, 5.4, 6.3, 8.2, 8.4, 10.1 and 10.5. In 5.2 and 10.1 there is a gold drop under each ear, on both sides of the face.

minors.description: Nagoji's staging breaks between two walking beats. He walks into the hall in 2.1 and walks down the lane in 2.5, but in 2.3 he looks seated or crouched, with both bandaged forearms laid flat across his knees at the bottom of the frame.
minors.evidence: Bottom of 2.3: both bandaged forearms lie horizontally across the frame at knee height, with the dhoti bunched below them.

minors.description: The hall's open side switches between panels on the same page. In 4.2 and 4.3 (reverse angles) the sea is on screen right, but in 4.4 the sea and pillars are on screen left behind Nagoji, who still faces the king. In the platform two-shots 5.3 and 5.5, palms and sea appear behind the king and diwan. In 2.2 and 6.1 that wall is closed, with the red conch banner.
minors.evidence: 4.4: ocean and balustrade at the left edge. 4.3: palm and sky at the right. 5.3: palms and water over a balustrade between Varma and Ramayyan. 2.2: a solid wall with a hanging conch banner behind the platform.

minors.description: The view through the open side drifts away from the inlet, boats, sea and red stone wall set up in 1.3 and 7.3. In 3.1, 3.3, 4.2 and 6.4 a Deccan-style hilltop fort fills the opening instead of the sea; this is the known backdrop leak from the Nagoji sheet. In 9.2 a Portuguese colonial town with an arcaded villa and a bell tower shows across the water, and 10.3 has a similar white, red-roofed town. Either could make the reader think of Goa.
minors.evidence: 9.2, left edge: white arcaded buildings with red roofs and a domed bell tower. 6.4: a tan hilltop fortress behind the red-turbaned guards. 3.3: a hill fort over palms where the sea should be.

minors.description: The script locks Varma's jewelled peacock-feather crest for every panel of this audience, but some panels lose it. In 9.4 the turban is cut by the panel top and no crest shows. In 8.5 the top of the turban is cropped and the crest is gone. In 3.3 the jewel is there but no feather.
minors.evidence: 9.4 crop: cream-and-gold turban band over the forehead, no jewel or feather. 8.5: the turban is cut off at the frame edge just above the brow.

minors.description: The palace guards change costume from scene to scene. In 1.4, 5.1 and 6.1 they are bare-headed, with a topknot or hair tied back, and crossed leather belts over a white mundu; in 1.4 and 5.1 they are bare-chested. In 6.4 the guards wear red turbans and white tunics with crossed belts, which reads like a later sepoy uniform and does not match the rest of the hall.
minors.evidence: 6.4: three spear guards in maroon-red turbans, white tunics and crossed brown belts. 1.4: bare-chested guards with topknots and crossed straps.

minors.description: The writing props and the map move around. In the 4.5 inset Ramayyan writes with a brass pen-like stylus on what looks like a wooden plank, not the palm leaf the script asks for and that the palm-leaf bundles elsewhere establish. The map lies on the mat before Varma in 2.2, but in 5.3 it is spread on Ramayyan's table.
minors.evidence: 4.5 inset: a gold-coloured pointed pen on a wood-grain board. 5.3: Varma's finger on a map that lies on Ramayyan's table, next to his palm-leaf bundle and ink pot.

minors.description: Ibrahim's scar is drawn as a fresh red cut rather than an old healed scar. This is the known fault on the Ibrahim sheet. The scar is correctly on his LEFT side, from the ear to the jaw.
minors.evidence: Zoomed 2.3 and 1.2: a thin pinkish-red line running down from in front of the left ear through the beard.

minors.description: The background guards wear a uniform that reads like later British East India Company sepoys, not Travancore guards. CONTINUITY.md asks for regular troops in white mundu with crossed leather belts, and says Indian troops must not read as British troops. They also don't match the guards elsewhere in this chapter.
minors.evidence: Four guards behind Ibrahim and the pillars (left third and center of the panel) wear matching red turbans with a pinned badge, long white tunics, red cloth crossbelts and red cummerbunds. Together that is a regimental sepoy livery. Guards elsewhere in the chapter (1.4, 3.1, 5.1, 5.2, 10.1) are bare-chested or in white, with brown leather crossbelts and white or no turbans.

minors.description: Through the open side of Varma's hall, the background shows what reads as a Portuguese colonial town (the Goa look) instead of the Travancore coast. Ch8 8.2 uses the same skyline for Portuguese Chaul. 10.3 repeats the effect.
minors.evidence: Left edge of 9.2, below the [in Malayalam] balloon: a whitewashed church-style tower with an onion cupola, plus a cluster of whitewashed villas with red tiled roofs and arched loggias on the shore. 10.3 has a similar cluster of whitewashed red-roofed villas behind Nagoji's bandaged hand on the right.

minors.description: Directly behind the Travancore gate stands a European-style colonial mansion. It clashes with the laterite wall and the carved timber hall shown in 1.3, and suggests a Portuguese settlement at the Travancore gate.
minors.evidence: Background center, between Nagoji's head and Ibrahim's turban: a whitewashed two-storey building with rows of regular rectangular windows, a red tiled hip roof and a small tiled turret. It sits above the red laterite inner wall and the guards' spear points.

minors.description: Background figures on the quay are dressed in what reads as 20th-century workwear, which is an anachronism for 1738 to 1753.
minors.evidence: In the strip of shore behind the two whisperers, just under the Ramayyan caption: one man wears a khaki short-sleeved shirt with a shoulder strap and belted khaki trousers. The man next to him wears a short-sleeved button shirt over trousers. A third figure at far left wears a short-sleeved white shirt.

minors.description: Poor balloon fit: the 13-word line 'He says you speak as if you have counted men and ships for years.' is set as a tall, narrow column of 8 lines of 1 to 2 words each, with the balloon pressed against the panel's top border. The second balloon is pressed against the right border.
minors.evidence: In the first balloon, 'He says / you speak / as if you / have / counted / men and / ships for / years.' runs top to bottom of the panel. Its top touches the frame line. The lower balloon's right edge sits about 5 px from the right border.

minors.description: Crowded attribution. Ramayyan's first balloon sits squarely over Varma's torso, and its tail aims at the gap between the two men rather than clearly at Ramayyan. His second balloon is a narrow 7-line column covering his whole torso.
minors.evidence: The tail of 'He says they already have horse from the Nayak of Madurai...' ends at Ramayyan's left shoulder edge, right beside Varma's necklaces. 'They have Dutch fortifications in their minds...' wraps to 7 short lines.

minors.description: Ramayyan's long off-panel balloon covers much of the sea and shoreline in the view the script says must 'plant clearly' the Chapter 7 ground. Its tail runs to the far top-right corner, an odd place for Ramayyan, who is inside the hall.
minors.evidence: The balloon covers the centre-right of the beach and sea view. The laterite bluff and the near strip of sand stay visible lower-left of it. The tail rises diagonally to the panel's top-right corner.

minors.description: Reading order and tail are ambiguous. Nagoji's off-panel balloon has a long tail running down to the bottom border over the map beside Varma's pointing finger, so it reads as pointing at the map. Ramayyan's 'Here. This river mouth...' sits directly below it on the left, so a reader scanning down may read the translation before the '[in Malayalam]' balloon at right. Both balloons also overlap the inset's edges.
minors.evidence: The tail ends on the map's coastline at the bottom border. '[in Malayalam]' is at mid-right; 'Here. This river mouth' is at lower left beneath the Nagoji balloon. The inset's right edge and bottom are covered by balloons.

minors.description: Two stacked inset rows of different widths leave ragged left and right edges down the middle of the page.
minors.evidence: Measured extents: 4.3 runs 310-1527 and 4.4 runs 370-1467, against page margins of 148-1688. The rows above and below run to the full margins.

minors.description: Inconsistent row widths. 3.1 is slightly narrower than the rows below it, and 3.5 is a much narrower floating panel centred on the page, so the left and right edges step in and out. Separately, in 3.1 the second Ibrahim balloon's tail lands on his outstretched hand over Nagoji's bowing back instead of on Ibrahim's head.
minors.evidence: Measured extents: 3.1 runs 178-1658, 3.2 to 3.4 run 148-1688, and 3.5 runs 364-1472. In 3.1, the tail of 'He comes from Portuguese chains...' ends at Ibrahim's fingertips, next to Nagoji's shoulder.

minors.description: Panel 5.5 is inset top and bottom relative to its neighbour 5.4, so the bottom row's borders do not line up. Separately, the script's balloon modifiers are not lettered: 5.3 VARMA (sharp) gets a plain round balloon rather than a jagged one, and 5.5 RAMAYYAN (soft) gets a full-size standard balloon.
minors.evidence: At x 1300, 5.5's top border is at y about 1683 and its bottom at about 2519. At x 300, 5.4's are at about 1660 and 2541, a step of about 22 px at each end. The 5.3 '[in Malayalam]' balloon has the same outline as every other balloon.

minors.description: The script calls for 1.3 to be 'the largest panel on the page' and for Ibrahim's off-panel line to be small and soft. Instead 1.3 is the same size as 1.2, and the line is set in a full-size standard balloon whose tail is jammed into the bottom-left corner of the frame.
minors.evidence: 1.2 and 1.3 split the second row equally. The 'This is only one claw...' balloon is the same size and weight as Ibrahim's balloons in 1.2, and its tail tip touches the left border near the bottom corner.

minors.description: Tail ambiguity: both Ibrahim balloons aim at the seam between Nagoji's and Ibrahim's heads. The first tail ends on Nagoji's hair just in front of Ibrahim's nose, so it could be read as Nagoji speaking.
minors.evidence: The tail of 'Marthanda Varma. And his diwan.' ends on the back of Nagoji's curly hair. The tail of 'Remember what I said about gifts.' points up between the two faces.

minors.description: The script asks for open hall space and rafters above Nagoji for the balloons. Instead his head is pressed against the top border and the balloons flank his face. In 8.1 his head is likewise clipped at the top frame.
minors.evidence: In 8.4 the crown of Nagoji's hair touches the top border, with the two balloons on either side of his face. In 8.1 his hair is cut by the top border.

minors.description: On the chapter's closing image, the top border clips the crown of Nagoji's head. The 'separate, weighted' final caption is set in the same plain box as every other caption, butting the top border right in his eyeline up the coast.
minors.evidence: Nagoji's hair is cut at the top frame line. The caption 'For now, Travancore was the forge...' begins immediately right of his profile, at the top border, with no distinct styling.

minors.description: The scripted gesture is missing. Nagoji should be shaping a low wall in the air with one bandaged hand while he describes the bastions. He is cropped at the chest and neither hand is visible.
minors.evidence: page-04.png, panel 4.3 (x 225-1100, y 748-1012). Nagoji's head and shoulders sit at the bottom centre (about x 490-660) and the frame ends at his collar.

minors.description: The script makes the arrival establishing shot (inlet, red-stone wall, pillared hall, inland rampart) 'the largest panel on the page'. In the render it is a half-width panel exactly the size of 1.2, and the gate panel 1.4 is bigger.
minors.evidence: page-01.png: 1.2 and 1.3 are both about 550x615 (side by side, y 545-1155). 1.4 is full width, about 1110x415.

minors.description: The scripted lighting beat does not show. 7.1 says the sea light from the open side catches the scar along Ibrahim's LEFT jaw. No scar is visible on his face in this panel.
minors.evidence: page-07.png, panel 7.1. Ibrahim's face (about x 340-420, y 300-390) shows a beard and a turban, but no scar line on either jaw, although it is visible in 1.2 and 2.3.

minors.description: The script ends this panel with 'Through the open side, the sea', so the waiting hall still has the sea. On screen left there are only pillars and a sliver of palm, and no sea is visible.
minors.evidence: page-06.png, panel 6.1 (x 108-660, y 258-795). The left edge shows pillars, a standing guard and a palm frond at about x 110-160, y 380-470, with no water anywhere in the panel.

minors.description: The framing departs from the script. 9.5 should be a high shot from the entrance end, with Nagoji small on his mat before a platform at the far end. The render is a low, side-on three-quarter view with Nagoji kneeling large at left and the dais at right, so the closing image of the verdict loses the 'small man before the platform' geometry.
minors.evidence: page-09.png, panel 9.5 (x 108-1218, y 1372-1832). The camera sits at about seated eye height, Nagoji is about 260px tall at x 195-370, and the platform sits on the right side rather than at the far end of the lane.

minors.description: Whitewashed European-style buildings appear in the background views: a two-storey villa with tiled roof behind the gate, and a white house beside the inlet. This works against the opening line 'They did not take me to a palace' and the script's purely Travancore fort (red stone wall, pillared hall, rampart).
minors.evidence: page-01.png 1.4: a white two-storey building with a hipped red-tile roof and rectangular windows above the gate wall (about x 520-660, y 1300-1400). page-07.png 7.3: a white red-roofed house behind the red wall (about x 345-445, y 1020-1050). page-09.png 9.2: a colonial-looking white town with a tower through the open side (about x 110-180, y 760-890).

minors.description: The first balloon sits over the exact point where Kanka and the riders hit the musketeer line ('felt it break'). The collision, which is the panel's payoff, is hidden.
minors.evidence: page-08.png, balloon 'What you do not yet have...' (about x 320-740, y 690-850). It covers the horses' forelegs and the gap between the charging horses and the falling musketeers in the centre of the 8.2 stain.

minors.description: The script's delivery marks are not lettered. VARMA (sharp) at 5.3, RAMAYYAN (soft) at 5.5 and IBRAHIM (small, soft) at 1.3 are all set as ordinary full-size balloons, so the king's sharp reaction before the translation reads only through the face.
minors.evidence: page-05.png: the 5.3 '[in Malayalam]' balloon (about x 800-980, y 645-730) is a standard smooth oval. 'Already marked, Maharaja.' (about x 935-1140, y 1280-1400) is standard size. page-01.png: 'This is only one claw' at 1.3 is a full-size balloon.

minors.description: Ramayyan's introduction panel, which the script's production notes make his reference frame for all later panels, crops off the top of his head. His defining receding hairline is not shown, and he reads as a man with a full head of curly hair. In 2.2, 3.1 and 5.3 he is clearly balding.
minors.evidence: page-02.png, panel 2.4. The panel's top border cuts Ramayyan's head at about y 1152, just above his brows (head at about x 590-700). Compare page-03.png 3.1 and page-05.png 5.3, where the bald crown is visible.
